y-m-65-01.title: When "choose two people" can mean two different things
y-m-65-01.topic: Permutations and combinations: the rule for treating chosen results as the same
y-m-65-01.goal: Explain that even for the same "choose 2 out of 5", the number of cases changes when the rule for telling results apart is different, and find the line with a double-counting error in a solution.
y-m-65-01.material:
Two people are chosen from 5 candidates (가, 나, 다, 라, 마). Each person can be chosen only once.
Situation ㄱ: The two chosen people take different positions, class president and vice president.
Situation ㄴ: The two chosen people together take the same role, class representatives.
You want to compare the number of cases in the two situations.
y-m-65-01.thinking.0: Check the rule for treating results as the same
y-m-65-01.thinking.1: Find the wrong line in a solution
y-m-65-01.thinking.2: Make your own examples and explain the rule for telling them apart
y-m-65-01.prereq.0: The H2/H3 label on this task is only a difficulty level assigned for production. It does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to that grade.
y-m-65-01.prereq.1: The product rule for counting (counting cases by multiplying)
y-m-65-01.prereq.2: Condition: the 5 candidates are all different people, and no one can be chosen twice
y-m-65-01.s.s1.prompt: What do you think now about the number of cases in the two situations ㄱ and ㄴ?
y-m-65-01.s.s1.hint.0: In ㄱ, write down separately the result "가 is president and 나 is vice president" and the result "나 is president and 가 is vice president."
y-m-65-01.s.s1.hint.1: Count in how many ways the same two people (가, 나) are written as results in ㄴ.
y-m-65-01.s.s1.explain: In ㄱ, (가 is president, 나 is vice president) and (나 is president, 가 is vice president) are different results, but in ㄴ they are the same two representatives, so it is one result. ㄱ has 20 cases and ㄴ has 10 cases.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.prompt: A student solved situation ㄴ like this. Choose the wrong line.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether each line says how many times a result was counted.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write down for yourself how many times (가, 나) and (나, 가) each appear in this solution's multiplication.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.line.0: Count the ways to choose 2 representatives from 5 candidates.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.line.2: (가, 나) and (나, 가) are the same representatives, but the multiplication above counts these two only once.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.line.3: Therefore the number of cases in situation ㄴ is 20.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.explain: 5×4 counts by telling "first, second" apart, so it counts (가, 나) and (나, 가) separately. Line 3, which says it "counts only once," is wrong, and because of that the 20 ways in line 4 is also wrong. The same pair of representatives was counted 2 times each, so the answer is 10.
y-m-65-01.s.s3.prompt: Make up one situation where the order (role) must be told apart when counting and one where it must not, and write the rule for telling them apart in one sentence.
y-m-65-01.s.s3.hint.0: For each situation, first ask: "If the two people swap places, does the result change?"
y-m-65-01.s.s3.hint.1: Think of a case where the people chosen first are each assigned to different jobs (for example, reading a book, giving a presentation) and a case where they all do the same job.
y-m-65-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the situations you made distinguish the two rules for telling results apart?
y-m-65-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you test for yourself whether swapping places changes the result?
y-m-65-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you work out the number of cases as a number?
y-m-65-01.s.s3.model.0: Example where order is told apart: choosing a presenter and a host from 5 people. If the two people swap roles, it is a different result, so order is told apart. Example where order is not told apart: choosing 2 cleaning duty students from 5 people. The two do the same job, so swapping places gives the same result.
y-m-65-01.s.s3.model.1: Deciding who gets 1st and 2nd place in a race is a case where a different order gives a different result, while choosing 2 people to run in the same group is a case where order does not matter, since swapping the order still gives the same group, so order is not told apart.

y-m-65-02.title: The same 8 moves, but a different road shape
y-m-65-02.topic: Number of paths: the same number of moves, different maps
y-m-65-02.goal: Understand that even with the same number of moves, the number of shortest paths changes depending on how the moves are split between right and up, and make a map that meets the condition yourself.
y-m-65-02.material: To go from home to school, you must move a times to the right (→) and b times up (↑), for a total of a+b=8 moves. Each map has different a and b. You move only one square at a time, only to the right or up, and no road is blocked. A shortest path can be written as a line of 8 symbols made of → and ↑.
y-m-65-02.thinking.0: Turn a path into an arrangement of symbols
y-m-65-02.thinking.1: Make several maps that meet the condition
y-m-65-02.thinking.2: Decide whether the information is enough
y-m-65-02.prereq.0: The H2/H3 label on this task is only a difficulty level assigned for production. It does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to that grade.
y-m-65-02.prereq.1: Experience counting paths by arranging items with repeats or by combinations
y-m-65-02.prereq.2: Condition: move one square at a time, only to the right or up, and every intersection can be passed (nothing is blocked)
y-m-65-02.s.s1.prompt: Between the map with (a, b)=(4, 4) and the map with (2, 6), which one do you think has more shortest paths?
y-m-65-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write down a few lines that arrange 2 → symbols and 6 ↑ symbols in 8 spaces.
y-m-65-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how many ways there are to first choose the spaces for → on the two maps.
y-m-65-02.s.s1.explain: For (4, 4), you choose 4 spaces out of 8 for →, so there are 70 ways; for (2, 6), you choose 2 spaces for →, so there are 28 ways.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 maps (a, b) with different shapes where a+b=8 and there are at least 50 shortest paths. (A map with a and b swapped is treated as the same shape.)
y-m-65-02.s.s2.hint.0: Put in a=0, 1, 2, ... one at a time and compare the number of ways to choose the spaces for →.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.hint.1: First find the number of paths for the map with the smallest value and the one with the largest value, then narrow down toward the middle value.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are integers that are 0 or greater.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be integers that are 0 or greater.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The total number of moves is 8.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.ok.c3: This map has at least 50 shortest paths.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.fail.c3: This map does not have 50 shortest paths.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.explain: (4, 4) has 70 ways, and (3, 5) and (5, 3) have 56 ways. (2, 6) has 28 ways and (1, 7) has 8 ways, which are not enough.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain how you found the number of shortest paths for the one map you chose.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: If you write a path as a line of → and ↑, think about what you need to decide so that the line is fixed.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Test whether there are cases where swapping → and ↑ gives the same path.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Is it clear why you turned the path into a line of 8 spaces?
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you take into account that swapping → symbols with each other gives the same path?
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you work out the actual number with the method you wrote?
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.model.0: This is the problem of choosing 3 spaces out of 8 for →, so it is the number of ways to choose 3 out of 8, which is 56 ways.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.model.1: It is the number of ways to arrange 3 → symbols and 5 ↑ symbols in a line, but swapping the same symbols gives the same path, so you divide 8! by 3! and 5! to get 56.
y-m-65-02.s.s3.prompt: On the (4, 4) map, one intersection is closed for construction and cannot be passed. What must you know in order to find the number of shortest paths?
y-m-65-02.s.s3.hint.0: Think separately about the paths blocked by the construction and the paths not blocked.
y-m-65-02.s.s3.explain: The number of paths that are removed depends on which intersection is blocked. For example, an intersection right next to the start and an intersection near the destination are passed by very different numbers of paths.

y-m-65-03.title: Are there two people in the class with the same birthday?
y-m-65-03.topic: Complement events and multiplying probabilities: the probability of at least one matching pair
y-m-65-03.goal: Explain why the probability of "at least one" is found from the opposite case instead of counting directly, and decide how the probability changes when the assumptions change.
y-m-65-03.material: In a class of 30 students, you want to find out whether there are two or more students with the same birthday. Model: every student's birthday is one of 365 days, each day is equally likely, and students do not affect each other. The year is not considered.
y-m-65-03.thinking.1: Revise your judgment with new information
y-m-65-03.thinking.2: Check the assumptions of the model
y-m-65-03.prereq.0: The H2/H3 label on this task is only a difficulty level assigned for production. It does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to that grade.
y-m-65-03.prereq.1: The product of the probabilities of independent events
y-m-65-03.prereq.3: Condition: a birthday is one of 365 days (excluding February 29), every day is equally likely, and students' birthdays are assumed to be independent of each other
y-m-65-03.s.s1.prompt: Let's think step by step about the probability that there is at least one pair of students with the same birthday.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write in one line what information your prediction was based on.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the new information is strong enough to change your prediction or whether it can stay the same.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.0.info: In a class of 30, how likely do you think it is that there is at least one pair with the same birthday? You have not calculated yet.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which is closest to your intuition?
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.0.after: Here, either answer is just intuition. What matters is that 30 people make 435 pairs.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This assumed that 365 days is far more than 30 people, so they hardly ever overlap.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This assumed that overlaps happen once in a while.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This took into account that the number of pairs is large.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.1.info: These are the results of calculating the probability for small groups. 5 people: about 2.7%, 10 people: about 11.7%, 20 people: about 41.1%, 23 people: about 50.7%.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: What is your guess for 30 people now?
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.1.after: The probability increases as the number of people grows, and it already passes 50% at 23 people, so for 30 people it is larger than that.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This assumed that the increase grows in a straight line as people are added.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This continued the upward trend that passes 50% at 23 people.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This assumed that the probability can decrease even as people are added.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.2.info:
The probability that all 30 people have different birthdays is (365/365)×(364/365)×...×(336/365), which is about 29.4%. So the probability that there is at least one matching pair is 1 minus this, about 70.6%.
Now think about reality. Real students' birthdays are not spread evenly over the seasons and are concentrated in certain months.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: If birthdays are concentrated, how does the probability of at least one matching pair compare with 70.6%?
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.2.after: The even case has the fewest overlaps. If there is concentration, the chance of the same day overlapping is the same or greater. So 70.6% is likely lower than the real value.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This assumed that with concentration they avoid each other.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This assumed that the calculation is the same even if the model changes.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It does not become smaller than 70.6%
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This assumed that with concentration the same days overlap more often.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.reflect: Look back at how you revised your first intuition after the calculation result and the change in assumptions, or what information let you keep it.
y-m-65-03.s.s2.prompt: Explain why you use "all different" instead of counting the probability of "at least one matching pair" directly.
y-m-65-03.s.s2.hint.0: If you list the cases with a matching pair directly, write down a few of the different forms they can take.
y-m-65-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the "all different" case is a single form.
y-m-65-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is your reason for why direct counting is hard specific?
y-m-65-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you connect the reason for subtracting from 1 to the fact that the probabilities add up to 1?
y-m-65-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you think about whether the same method works for numbers of people other than 30?
y-m-65-03.s.s2.model.0: The cases with a matching pair come in too many forms, such as only one pair matching, two pairs matching, or three people matching, so they are hard to count directly. The opposite, "all different," has just one form, so it can be found directly by multiplication, and subtracting from 1 makes it easy.
y-m-65-03.s.s2.model.1: The total probability is 1, so you can find the probability that no pair is the same and subtract it from 1. You only need to find the all-different case, so the calculation is much simpler.
y-m-65-03.s.s2.modelNote.1: It does not use the words "complement event," but it is the same idea.

y-m-65-04.title: Does a ball put aside without looking affect the next ball?
y-m-65-04.topic: Conditional probability: does the probability change when you get information?
y-m-65-04.goal: Tell apart how the probability of the same event changes when you know information and when you do not, and build a bag setup that meets the condition yourself.
y-m-65-04.material: A bag has 6 white balls and 4 black balls. The balls have the same shape and are well mixed. You take out one ball, put it aside without looking at its color, and then take out another ball.
y-m-65-04.thinking.0: Judge how information affects the probability
y-m-65-04.thinking.2: Build a model that fits the condition
y-m-65-04.prereq.0: The H2/H3 label on this task is only a difficulty level assigned for production. It does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to that grade.
y-m-65-04.prereq.1: The basic idea of probability, the multiplication rule, or the meaning of conditional probability
y-m-65-04.prereq.2: Condition: every ball is equally likely to be picked, and a ball that is taken out is not put back
y-m-65-04.s.s1.prompt: If you do not know the color of the ball put aside, what is the probability that the second ball taken out is white?
y-m-65-04.s.s1.hint.1: Multiply the probabilities of each case and add them, then compare with the original 6/10.
y-m-65-04.s.s1.r.a: This looked only at the reduced number of balls and did not consider that the color is unknown.
y-m-65-04.s.s1.explain: If the first ball is white (6/10), the probability that the second is white is 5/9; if it is black (4/10), it is 6/9. (6/10)(5/9)+(4/10)(6/9)=54/90=6/10.
y-m-65-04.s.s2.prompt: You found out that the ball put aside is white. Now what is the probability that the second ball is white?
y-m-65-04.s.s2.hint.0: Count again the balls left in the bag, separately as white and black.
y-m-65-04.s.s2.hint.1: Compare with the earlier 6/10 and say whether it is the same or different, with a reason.
y-m-65-04.s.s2.r.a: There are 9 balls left, but the number of white balls was not reduced.
y-m-65-04.s.s2.r.d: This reduced only the number of white balls without reducing the denominator.
y-m-65-04.s.s2.explain: If the ball put aside is white, the bag has 5 white balls and 4 black balls left, so it is 5/9.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.prompt: Build a new bag with 10 balls in total, w white balls and b black balls. Make 2 different setups such that, when you know the ball put aside is white, the probability that the second ball is white is at least 1/2 and there is at least 1 black ball.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.hint.0: Under the condition w+b=10, change w one at a time and calculate (w-1)/9.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.hint.1: Also find the cases where the smallest and largest values of w break the condition.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.ok.c1: The numbers of balls are integers.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.fail.c1: The numbers of balls must be integers.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.fail.c2: The number of balls is not 10.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.ok.c3: There is at least 1 black ball.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.fail.c3: There must be at least 1 black ball.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.ok.c4: When the ball put aside is white, the probability that the second ball is white is at least 1/2.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.explain: If w=6 it is 5/9, and if w=9 it is 8/9. If w=5 it is 4/9, which is less than 1/2, and if w=10 there are no black balls, so the condition is broken.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.because.prompt: Explain why the same "probability that the second ball is white" is calculated differently when you do not know the color of the ball put aside and when you do.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.because.hint.0: Write down what is left in the bag when you do not know and when you do.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.because.hint.1: Compare how the possible cases change when you have more information.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you give the reason for 6/10 when you do not know and the reason for 5/9 when you do?
y-m-65-04.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you take into account that information reduces the number of possible cases?
y-m-65-04.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Did you think about how, when you do not know the color, the first ball is in effect in the same position as the second ball?
y-m-65-04.s.s3.because.model.0: If you do not know the color of the ball put aside, the second ball is under the same conditions as drawing once at the start, so it is 6/10. If you know it is white, the situation is that only 5 white balls and 4 black balls are left, so it changes to 5/9.
y-m-65-04.s.s3.because.model.1: When you do not know the color, the ball put aside could be white or black, so the weighted average of the two is 6/10. When you learn that it is white, the black case disappears, so the probability changes.

y-m-65-05.title: Can we write this situation as B(n, p)?
y-m-65-05.topic: Assumptions of the binomial distribution model: independence and a constant probability of success
y-m-65-05.goal: Decide whether the assumptions of the binomial distribution model (independent trials, constant probability of success) hold in a situation, and redesign a situation where they do not hold so that the model fits.
y-m-65-05.thinking.0: Check the conditions of the model
y-m-65-05.prereq.0: The H2/H3 label on this task is only a difficulty level assigned for production. It does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to that grade.
y-m-65-05.prereq.1: The definition of the binomial distribution (independent trials, constant probability of success)
y-m-65-05.prereq.2: Condition: whether an item is defective, the color of a ball, and whether a shot goes in each have one of two outcomes
y-m-65-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the situations where you can say the binomial distribution can be used as it is.
y-m-65-05.s.s1.hint.0: In each situation, first check whether the probability of success is the same in every trial.
y-m-65-05.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the trials affect each other (whether an earlier result changes the probability of a later one).
y-m-65-05.s.s1.r.a: In (가), the probability of success is the same every time and the trials are independent.
y-m-65-05.s.s1.r.b: The balls are not put back, so the probability changes with each trial, but this assumed it is the same.
y-m-65-05.s.s1.r.c: An earlier result changes the probability of a later result, but this assumed they are independent.
y-m-65-05.s.s2.prompt: A student solved (나) using the binomial distribution. Choose the wrong line.
y-m-65-05.s.s2.hint.0: Look for whether each line says "the probability is the same every time."
y-m-65-05.s.s2.hint.1: Work out for yourself whether it is possible for all 4 draws to be white when there are only 3 white balls.
y-m-65-05.s.s2.line.0: In (나), the probability that the first ball taken out is black is 7/10.
y-m-65-05.s.s2.line.1: There are 4 draws, so n=4, and the probability of a black ball each time is 7/10, so it follows B(4, 7/10).
y-m-65-05.s.s2.line.2: So the probability of 0 black balls is (3/10)^4=0.0081.
y-m-65-05.s.s2.explain: Line 2 says it is 7/10 every time, but the balls are not put back, so the probability changes. The result in line 3 is also wrong. There are only 3 white balls, so all 4 draws cannot be white, and the probability of 0 black balls is actually 0.
y-m-65-05.s.s3.prompt: Write at least one way to change how the experiment is done so that (나) can be treated with the binomial distribution, and explain why the model's assumptions hold after the change.
y-m-65-05.s.s3.hint.0: Check again the assumption that was the problem (whether the probability is the same every time).
y-m-65-05.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what to do with the ball taken out so that the makeup of the bag is the same every time.
y-m-65-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your changed method directly fix the assumption that was the problem?
y-m-65-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you state n and p after the change?
y-m-65-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you compare with another method (when there are very many balls)?
y-m-65-05.s.s3.model.0: If you put the ball back and mix each time, the probability of a black ball is the same 7/10 every time and the draws are independent, so B(4, 7/10) can be used.
y-m-65-05.s.s3.model.1: If the bag has so many balls that taking one out hardly changes the proportion, the binomial distribution can be used as an approximation.
y-m-65-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: This answer says that it is an approximation.

y-m-65-06.title: How you choose the 30 students changes the result
y-m-65-06.topic: Sample survey: sampling methods and representativeness
y-m-65-06.goal: Understand that not only the size of the sample but also the way it is chosen affects how representative the result is, decide what more you need to know to state a conclusion, and design a better sampling method.
y-m-65-06.material:
In a school with 600 students, you want to find the proportion of students who agree with the idea "Let's make lunchtime 15 minutes longer."
Method 가: Ask the first 30 students to arrive at the cafeteria.
Method 나: Randomly choose 30 students by computer from the student number list and ask them.
Method 다: Post a survey on the school website and get answers from students who respond on their own (142 students responded).
y-m-65-06.thinking.1: Decide what information is needed for a conclusion
y-m-65-06.prereq.0: The H2/H3 label on this task is only a difficulty level assigned for production. It does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to that grade.
y-m-65-06.prereq.1: The meaning of population and sample
y-m-65-06.prereq.2: Condition: there are 600 students in total, the number of students in each grade is the same, and no information that identifies individuals is collected
y-m-65-06.s.s1.prompt: Which of the three methods gives the sample that would best represent the opinions of all students?
y-m-65-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write down which students are likely to end up in the sample under each method.
y-m-65-06.s.s1.hint.1: Consider whether the students who end up in the sample are likely to think the same about lunchtime.
y-m-65-06.s.s1.explain: In Method 나, every student is equally likely to be chosen, so bias is reduced. Method 가 can lean toward students who go early, and Method 다 toward students with strong opinions.
y-m-65-06.s.s2.prompt: In Method 다, 110 of the 142 students agreed (about 77%). To say from this result that "about 77% of all students agree," what else do you need to know?
y-m-65-06.s.s2.hint.0: Imagine what kind of students the 110 who agreed might have been.
y-m-65-06.s.s2.hint.1: Consider what the 458 students who did not respond might think.
y-m-65-06.s.s2.o.b: Whether 142 respondents is a large enough number
y-m-65-06.s.s2.r.b: This looked only at the size and did not consider who the respondents are.
y-m-65-06.s.s2.explain: Students who respond on their own may be students who are very unhappy with lunchtime. You can generalize only if there is evidence that students who responded and students who did not think similarly.
y-m-65-06.s.s3.prompt: Fix Method 가 by designing a way of choosing students so that the sample represents all students better, and write why you choose them that way.
y-m-65-06.s.s3.hint.0: First write down which students are left out or over-represented in Method 가.
y-m-65-06.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what procedure is needed to give every student a chance of being chosen.
y-m-65-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you mention a list or procedure that includes all students?
y-m-65-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you think about the limits of your method (students who are left out)?
y-m-65-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you separate what would change and what would not change if you made the size larger than 30?
y-m-65-06.s.s3.model.0: If you randomly choose 30 students by computer from a list with all the student numbers, the bias of choosing only students who go to the cafeteria early disappears, so it is easier to represent everyone.
y-m-65-06.s.s3.model.1: If you choose randomly within each grade in proportion to the number of students in each grade, you can avoid leaning toward one grade.

y-m-65-07.title: Identical candies and different candies
y-m-65-07.topic: Distributing identical items and distributing different items
y-m-65-07.goal: Decide that the number of cases changes depending on whether the objects are the same or different, and make and count, without missing any, the distributions that meet the condition.
y-m-65-07.material:
You give out all 6 candies to three people, 갑, 을, and 병. First think of the case where someone may receive no candy.
(가) All the candies look exactly the same.
(나) All the candies are different flavors.
y-m-65-07.thinking.0: Decide whether the objects are told apart
y-m-65-07.thinking.1: List every case that meets the condition without missing any
y-m-65-07.prereq.0: The H2/H3 label on this task is only a difficulty level assigned for production. It does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to that grade.
y-m-65-07.prereq.1: The sum rule and the product rule
y-m-65-07.prereq.2: Condition: the people 갑, 을, and 병 are three people who are told apart from each other, and all the candies are given out
y-m-65-07.s.s1.prompt: How do the numbers of cases in (가) and (나) compare?
y-m-65-07.s.s1.hint.0: In (가), check whether you only need to decide "who gets how many."
y-m-65-07.s.s1.hint.1: In (나), count the ways of deciding who each candy goes to, one candy at a time.
y-m-65-07.s.s1.explain: In (나), each candy goes to one of three people, so there are 3^6=729 ways; in (가), only the combinations of how many 갑, 을, and 병 receive are counted, so there are 28 ways.
y-m-65-07.s.s2.prompt: (가) All the candies are identical, and you give them out so that all three people receive at least 1 candy and no one receives more than 3. Make 4 different distributions of the numbers (x, y, z) that 갑, 을, and 병 receive. (If the people are different, it is a different distribution.)
y-m-65-07.s.s2.hint.0: First work out how many candies the person who gets the most can have in x+y+z=6.
y-m-65-07.s.s2.ok.c2: All the candies were given out.
y-m-65-07.s.s2.fail.c3: One or more people receive none.
y-m-65-07.s.s2.explain: The possible distributions are the 6 ways from changing the order of (1,2,3) and 1 way for (2,2,2), 7 ways in total.
y-m-65-07.s.s3.prompt: How many distributions are there in total that meet the conditions above (everyone gets at least 1, at most 3)?
y-m-65-07.s.s3.r.d: This looked only at the "at least 1" condition and missed the limit of 3.
y-m-65-07.s.s3.explain: There are 3!=6 ways to assign (1,2,3) to 갑, 을, and 병 and 1 way for (2,2,2), so 7 ways. If the only condition were "at least 1," there would be 10 ways.

y-m-65-08.title: Choosing a locker password format
y-m-65-08.topic: Product rule: designing a password format
y-m-65-08.goal: Compare numbers of cases by multiplying the number of choices for each slot, design formats that satisfy a constraint yourself, and decide how the number of cases changes when the condition changes.
y-m-65-08.material: A locker password has 5 slots in all. The first L slots are capital English letters (26 choices, A to Z), and the remaining D slots are digits (10 choices, 0 to 9). The same letter or digit may be used more than once. The format is set by L+D=5, with all letter slots first and the digit slots after.
y-m-65-08.thinking.0: Compare the number of cases for different slot makeups
y-m-65-08.thinking.1: Find several formats within a range constraint
y-m-65-08.thinking.2: Decide the effect of a change in the condition
y-m-65-08.prereq.0: The H2/H3 label on this task is only a difficulty level assigned for production. It does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to that grade.
y-m-65-08.prereq.2: Condition: the same letter may be repeated, there are 26 choices for a capital letter and 10 for a digit. There are 5 slots, with the capital letter slots first and the digit slots after
y-m-65-08.s.s1.prompt: (가) 2 letter slots + 3 digit slots, (나) 3 letter slots + 2 digit slots. Which format has more possible passwords?
y-m-65-08.s.s1.hint.0: For each format, write down the number of choices for each slot.
y-m-65-08.s.s1.hint.1: Compare by how many times the number of choices changes when you change one slot.
y-m-65-08.s.s1.o.a: It is (나). It has one more letter slot
y-m-65-08.s.s1.r.a: This focused on the fact that a letter slot has more choices than a digit slot.
y-m-65-08.s.s1.o.b: It is (가). It has one more digit slot
y-m-65-08.s.s1.r.b: This focused only on the number of slots rather than the kind of slot.
y-m-65-08.s.s1.o.c: They are the same. This is because there are 5 slots in both
y-m-65-08.s.s1.r.c: This looked only at the total number of slots and missed that the number of choices differs from slot to slot.
y-m-65-08.s.s2.prompt: Choose the number of letter slots L and the number of digit slots D so that the number of cases for the password is between 1 million and 5 million, inclusive. Make 2 different formats.
y-m-65-08.s.s2.hint.0: Change L one at a time from 0 to 5 and find the number of cases.
y-m-65-08.s.s2.hint.1: Find out whether some formats are ruled out because of the lower limit or the upper limit of the range.
y-m-65-08.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of slots are integers that are 0 or greater.
y-m-65-08.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of slots must be integers that are 0 or greater.
y-m-65-08.s.s2.fail.c2: There must be 5 slots in all.
y-m-65-08.s.s2.ok.c3: The number of cases is between 1 million and 5 million, inclusive.
y-m-65-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The number of cases is not between 1 million and 5 million.
y-m-65-08.s.s2.explain: If L=3 it is 1,757,600, and if L=4 it is 4,569,760. L=2 gives 676,000, which is not enough, and L=5 gives 11,881,376, which is over 5 million.
y-m-65-08.s.s2.because.prompt: For the one format you chose, write how you found the total number of passwords.
y-m-65-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: First write down the number of choices for each slot.
y-m-65-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about whether the choices for the slots affect each other.
y-m-65-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write the number of choices for each slot correctly?
y-m-65-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Do you understand why you multiply instead of add?
y-m-65-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you check your calculation result?
y-m-65-08.s.s2.because.model.0: The 3 letter slots each have 26 choices and the 2 digit slots each have 10 choices, so it is 26×26×26×10×10=1,757,600.
y-m-65-08.s.s2.because.model.1: You multiply because choosing for each slot does not affect the others. Multiplying 26 four times and 10 once gives 456,976×10=4,569,760.
y-m-65-08.s.s3.prompt: In the format (L, D)=(3, 2), if the rule is changed to "the 3 letter slots may be anywhere among the 5 slots," how many times the original is the number of cases? (Passwords that differ only in where the letter slots and digit slots are placed count as different passwords.)
y-m-65-08.s.s3.hint.0: Write down a few arrangements of where the letter slots can be placed.
y-m-65-08.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether different position arrangements could produce the same password twice.
y-m-65-08.s.s3.r.a: This saw the position arrangements as about two kinds.
y-m-65-08.s.s3.r.b: This took the number of positions for the letter slots to be 5.
y-m-65-08.s.s3.r.c: The ways to choose the slots for the 3 letter slots number 10 and do not overlap.
y-m-65-08.s.s3.r.d: This counted twice by also considering the order of the position arrangements.
y-m-65-08.s.s3.explain: The number of ways to choose the positions of 3 letter slots among 5 slots is 10, and different position arrangements give different passwords, so it is 1,757,600×10=17,576,000 ways.

y-m-65-09.title: If scores are re-marked, what happens to the mean and the spread?
y-m-65-09.topic: Linear transformation of a random variable: mean and standard deviation
y-m-65-09.goal: Know how the mean and standard deviation change when scores are converted by a linear expression, find the error in a transformation solution, and design a transformation that meets a goal yourself.
y-m-65-09.material: The mean of the scores X on a test is 60 and the standard deviation is 10. You want to re-mark the scores as Y = aX + b (a is a number greater than 0). That is, you multiply every score by a and then add b. The standard deviation is a value that shows how far the scores are from the mean on average.
y-m-65-09.thinking.0: Tell apart the effects of adding and multiplying
y-m-65-09.prereq.0: The H2/H3 label on this task is only a difficulty level assigned for production. It does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to that grade.
y-m-65-09.prereq.1: The meaning of mean and standard deviation (enough to explain the changes without mathematical formulas)
y-m-65-09.prereq.2: Condition: a is positive, the mean of X is 60, and the standard deviation is 10. The new score is Y=aX+b
y-m-65-09.s.s1.prompt: You add 10 points to every student to make Y = X + 10. What are the mean and standard deviation?
y-m-65-09.s.s1.hint.0: Using the scores of two students, check whether the gap between scores changes when all scores rise by the same amount.
y-m-65-09.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate for yourself, using the scores of a few students, how the mean changes.
y-m-65-09.s.s1.r.a: This assumed that the added value is added directly to both the mean and the standard deviation.
y-m-65-09.s.s1.r.b: This understood that the mean rises too and the gap between scores stays the same.
y-m-65-09.s.s1.r.c: This assumed that adding to every score does not change the mean.
y-m-65-09.s.s1.explain: If every score rises by the same amount, the mean rises by that amount too, but the gap between scores stays the same, so the standard deviation does not change.
y-m-65-09.s.s2.prompt: A student found the mean and standard deviation of Y = 1.5X − 10 like this. Choose the wrong line.
y-m-65-09.s.s2.hint.0: Look at whether each line says how "multiplying" and "subtracting" each act on the mean and the standard deviation.
y-m-65-09.s.s2.hint.1: Choose the scores of two students, convert them yourself, and check how the gap changes.
y-m-65-09.s.s2.line.1: The standard deviation of Y is 1.5×10−10=5.
y-m-65-09.s.s2.line.2: So the variance of Y is the square of 5, which is 25.
y-m-65-09.s.s2.explain: In line 2, the gap between scores changes only by the number multiplied and has nothing to do with the number subtracted. The standard deviation is 1.5×10=15 and the variance is 225. Line 3 is also wrong as a result.
y-m-65-09.s.s3.prompt: Make 3 different pairs (a, b) such that when you re-mark with Y = aX + b the mean becomes 70 points and the standard deviation is at most 12 points. (a is greater than 0.)
y-m-65-09.s.s3.hint.0: First write the relationship between a and b from the mean condition.
y-m-65-09.s.s3.hint.1: Separately find which range of a the standard deviation condition allows.
y-m-65-09.s.s3.fail.c2: The new mean is not 70 points.
y-m-65-09.s.s3.ok.c3: The new standard deviation is at most 12 points.
y-m-65-09.s.s3.fail.c3: The new standard deviation is over 12 points.
y-m-65-09.s.s3.explain: The mean condition is b=70−60a and the standard deviation condition is a≤1.2. If a=1 then b=10, if a=1.2 then b=−2, and if a=0.5 then b=40.
y-m-65-09.s.s3.because.prompt: Explain why b is fixed to one value once a is chosen, and why b plays no role in the standard deviation.
y-m-65-09.s.s3.because.hint.0: Write, using a and b, the expression that makes the mean 70.
y-m-65-09.s.s3.because.hint.1: Check whether the gap between scores changes when you change b with the same a.
y-m-65-09.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Do you say that b is determined from the mean equation 60a+b=70?
y-m-65-09.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write that b moves all scores by the same amount?
y-m-65-09.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Did you write that a stretches or shrinks the gap?
y-m-65-09.s.s3.because.model.0: For the new mean to be 70, 60a+b=70, so once you choose a, b is fixed as 70−60a. The standard deviation is proportional only to a, and b just moves all the scores by the same amount, so the gap does not change.
y-m-65-09.s.s3.because.model.1: For the mean to be 70, b is determined by a. Adding b moves the scores all together, so the spread stays the same, and multiplying by a makes the spread a times as large.

y-m-65-10.title: How accurate do we get if we increase the sample?
y-m-65-10.topic: Standard deviation of the sample mean: sample size and precision
y-m-65-10.goal: Use the fact that the spread of the sample mean is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size to design a sample size that meets a precision goal, and decide how to handle a goal that is impossible within the constraints.
y-m-65-10.material: The commuting times of the students of a school have an unknown mean but are known to have a standard deviation of 12 minutes. You want to estimate the overall mean by randomly choosing n students and finding the sample mean. The smaller the standard deviation of the sample mean (the standard error), the more precise the estimate. Because of the survey budget, n must be at most 100.
y-m-65-10.thinking.0: Predict the relationship between sample size and precision
y-m-65-10.prereq.0: The H2/H3 label on this task is only a difficulty level assigned for production. It does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to that grade.
y-m-65-10.prereq.1: When the population standard deviation is σ, the standard deviation of the mean of a sample of size n is σ/√n
y-m-65-10.prereq.2: Condition: the population standard deviation of 12 minutes is known, and the sample is assumed to be chosen randomly and independently
y-m-65-10.s.s1.prompt: If you make the sample size 4 times as large, what happens to the standard deviation of the sample mean?
y-m-65-10.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the values of 12/√n for n=9 and n=36 yourself.
y-m-65-10.s.s1.hint.1: Write how the square root part changes when you make the sample size 2 times and 4 times as large.
y-m-65-10.s.s1.r.a: This assumed it is inversely proportional to the size.
y-m-65-10.s.s1.r.b: This assumed that it has nothing to do with the sample size because the population is the same.
y-m-65-10.s.s1.r.c: This used the fact that it is inversely proportional to the square root of the size.
y-m-65-10.s.s1.r.d: This assumed that the spread grows as the sample gets larger.
y-m-65-10.s.s1.explain: The standard deviation of the sample mean is σ/√n, so when n becomes 4 times as large, the denominator becomes 2 times as large and the value becomes half.
y-m-65-10.s.s2.prompt: You want the standard deviation of the sample mean to be at most 2 minutes. Within the budget limit n≤100, make 3 different possible sample sizes n.
y-m-65-10.s.s2.hint.0: First find the smallest n that satisfies 12/√n ≤ 2.
y-m-65-10.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate the standard error yourself for the n that is 1 less and the n that is 1 more than that value.
y-m-65-10.s.s2.fail.c1: n must be a natural number.
y-m-65-10.s.s2.ok.c2: The standard error is at most 2 minutes.
y-m-65-10.s.s2.fail.c2: The standard error is greater than 2 minutes.
y-m-65-10.s.s2.ok.c3: It is within the budget limit.
y-m-65-10.s.s2.explain: If n=36 the standard error is exactly 2, and if n=100 it is 1.2. If n=35 it is about 2.03, which is not enough.
y-m-65-10.s.s3.prompt: This time you want to lower the standard error to at most 1 minute. Decide whether it is possible within the budget limit n≤100, and if not, suggest what to do.
y-m-65-10.s.s3.hint.0: First find the range of n that satisfies 12/√n ≤ 1.
y-m-65-10.s.s3.hint.1: Find the standard error when n=100 and compare it with the goal.
y-m-65-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate the n that is needed?
y-m-65-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you compare the standard error at n=100 with the goal?
y-m-65-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you make clear which value your alternative changes (the budget, the goal, the survey method)?
y-m-65-10.s.s3.model.0: For at most 1 minute, 12/√n≤1 requires n to be at least 144, so the limit of 100 students is not enough. You have to raise the budget limit or relax the goal to about 1.2 minutes.
y-m-65-10.s.s3.model.1: If n=100 the standard error is 1.2 minutes, which does not reach the goal of 1 minute. You can increase the budget or change the standard for the allowed error.
y-m-65-10.s.s3.modelNote.1: It skips the calculation of the needed n, but it has a judgment and an alternative.

y-m-65-11.title: A probability that depends on how the door was opened
y-m-65-11.topic: Conditional probability and the source of information: how the door is opened
y-m-65-11.goal: Decide that even in the same scene (one door is opened and a goat appears), the probability of success when switching changes if the information about how the door is opened changes, and explain why.
y-m-65-11.material: There are 3 doors. Behind one door is a car, and behind the other two doors are goats, and the car is equally likely to be behind each door. The contestant picks door 1, and then the host opens door 3 and a goat appears. The contestant may switch to door 2.
y-m-65-11.thinking.0: Check the source of the information
y-m-65-11.thinking.2: Compare different models of the same scene
y-m-65-11.prereq.0: The H2/H3 label on this task is only a difficulty level assigned for production. It does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to that grade.
y-m-65-11.prereq.1: The meaning of conditional probability (the sample space narrows)
y-m-65-11.prereq.2: Condition: the car is behind one of the 3 doors with equal probability, and behind the other doors there are goats. The contestant picks door 1
y-m-65-11.s.s1.prompt: Decide step by step how the probability of getting the car changes if you switch.
y-m-65-11.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write down the possible cases split into "when the car is behind door 1, door 2, and door 3."
y-m-65-11.s.s1.hint.1: Compare which cases the new information removes or how it changes their likelihood.
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.0.info: It is not known how the host chose door 3. All we know is that there was a goat behind door 3.
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you judge from the information known now?
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.0.after: The way the host opens a door is not known, so both "assuming it is the same" and "there is not enough information" are reasonable.
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This was certain that switching is better without any information.
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Switching or not switching is the same
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This assumed the two remaining doors are equally likely.
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This placed the advantage on the door chosen first.
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.0.o.d: There is not enough information to decide
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This saw that the host's way of acting is needed.
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now what is the probability of success if you switch?
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.1.after: The probability that the car is behind door 1 stays 1/3, and the probability 2/3 that it is behind door 2 or door 3 gathers on door 2, leaving out the opened door 3. Switching gives 2/3.
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This assumed the two remaining doors are equally likely.
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.2.info: A different way: the host does not know where the car is and opened one of door 2 and door 3 at random, and by chance a goat appeared (if the car had appeared, this scene would not have happened).
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.2.ask: In this way, what is the probability of success if you switch?
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.2.after: If door 1 is right and door 3 is opened, it is 1/3×1/2=1/6, and if door 2 is right and door 3 is opened, it is 1/3×1/2=1/6, which is the same. The case where door 3 has the car is gone, so doors 1 and 2 are each 1/2.
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This carried over the result of the earlier way as it is.
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This considered the chance that the opened door 3 has a goat and saw that doors 1 and 2 carry the same weight.
y-m-65-11.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This assumed the first choice is better.
y-m-65-11.s.s1.reflect: Look back at what you judged at first and how the information about the host's way of acting changed or kept that judgment.
y-m-65-11.s.s2.prompt: Explain why the probability of success when switching is different in the two host ways (opening knowingly and opening without knowing).
y-m-65-11.s.s2.hint.0: For each way, compare how likely it is that the event "door 3 is opened and a goat appears" happens depending on where the car is.
y-m-65-11.s.s2.hint.1: For each way, check whether the probability of that event happening depends on where the car is.
y-m-65-11.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say that the probability that door 3 is opened differs depending on where the car is?
y-m-65-11.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you tell apart whether the host's choice is information or not?
y-m-65-11.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you check by listing the cases yourself?
y-m-65-11.s.s2.model.0: If the host knows where the car is and opens a goat on purpose, it gives almost no clue about whether door 1 was right, so the probability piles onto door 2 and becomes 2/3. If the host opened at random and a goat happened to appear, the cases where the car is there split in two, 1/2 each.
y-m-65-11.s.s2.model.1: When the host opens knowingly, if the car is behind door 2 he can only open door 3, so the likelihood tilts to twice as much, but when he opens without knowing, the chance that door 3 is opened is the same whether door 1 or door 2 is right, so there is no information. That is why the probabilities differ.

y-m-65-12.title: If the density is 2, is the probability 2?
y-m-65-12.topic: Continuous random variable: the value of the probability density function and probability
y-m-65-12.goal: Understand that the value of a probability density function is not itself a probability, and make an interval yourself that meets the condition under which the density can be greater than 1.
y-m-65-12.material: A continuous random variable X follows a uniform distribution with a constant density on the interval from 0 to a. The graph is a rectangle with a constant height on this interval and is 0 outside. The total area of this shape is 1. A student claims, "If a=0.5, the density becomes 2, but a probability cannot be 2, so there is no such distribution."
y-m-65-12.thinking.0: Check the meaning of probability density
y-m-65-12.thinking.1: Find the error in the argument
y-m-65-12.thinking.2: Make an example that meets the condition
y-m-65-12.prereq.0: The H2/H3 label on this task is only a difficulty level assigned for production. It does not mean the curriculum assigns this subject to that grade.
y-m-65-12.prereq.1: The meaning of a continuous random variable and a probability density function (the probability of an interval is the area under the graph)
y-m-65-12.prereq.2: Condition: the problem deals with a uniform distribution whose probability density function has a constant value on the interval [0, a]. This task does not require integral calculation
y-m-65-12.s.s1.prompt: What do you think now about the student's claim?
y-m-65-12.s.s1.hint.0: Find the area of a rectangle with height 2 and width 0.5.
y-m-65-12.s.s1.hint.1: Write down what "the value of the density" and "the probability of an interval" each are on the graph.
y-m-65-12.s.s1.o.a: It is right. A probability cannot exceed 1, so there is no distribution with height 2
y-m-65-12.s.s1.r.a: This took the value of the density directly as a probability.
y-m-65-12.s.s1.explain: A probability is an area over an interval, and it is enough if the total area is 1. The height is 2 and the width is 0.5, so the area is 1.
y-m-65-12.s.s2.prompt: This student continued the claim like this. Choose the wrong line.
y-m-65-12.s.s2.hint.0: Check what each line uses the word "probability" for.
y-m-65-12.s.s2.hint.1: Find the probability on the interval [0, 0.25] as an area.
y-m-65-12.s.s2.line.1: The density of the uniform distribution with a=0.5 is 1/0.5=2.
y-m-65-12.s.s2.line.2: So in this distribution the probability at some value x would be 2, which is impossible.
y-m-65-12.s.s2.line.3: Therefore the uniform distribution with a=0.5 does not exist.
y-m-65-12.s.s2.explain: In line 3, reading the density 2 as a "probability" is wrong. For a continuous random variable, the probability at a single point is 0, and a probability is the area of an interval. The conclusion in line 4 that rests on this is also wrong.
y-m-65-12.s.s3.prompt: Make 3 different values of a such that the density 1/a of the uniform distribution on [0, a] is greater than 1 and the interval [0, 0.2] lies within the range of the distribution.
y-m-65-12.s.s3.hint.0: First find the range of a from the density 1/a>1.
y-m-65-12.s.s3.hint.1: Work out how large a must be at least for [0, 0.2] to lie within [0, a].
y-m-65-12.s.s3.fail.c2: The density is not greater than 1.
y-m-65-12.s.s3.ok.c3: The interval [0, 0.2] is within the range.
y-m-65-12.s.s3.explain: You can use a that is at least 0.2 and less than 1. If a=0.5 the density is 2, if a=0.25 the density is 4, and if a=0.8 the density is 1.25. If a=1 the density is 1, which is not greater than 1.
y-m-65-12.s.s3.because.prompt: Explain why the probability does not exceed 1 even though the density is greater than 1.
y-m-65-12.s.s3.because.hint.0: Find the probability of the interval [0.1, 0.2] using the height and the width.
y-m-65-12.s.s3.because.hint.1: Tell apart what the value of the density and the probability of an interval each are on the graph.
y-m-65-12.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you tell apart the difference between density and probability?
y-m-65-12.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you calculate it as the area of a rectangle?
y-m-65-12.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Did you recall that the probability at a single point is 0?
y-m-65-12.s.s3.because.model.0: The density is only a height, and the probability is the area over an interval. Even if the height is 2, the width is 0.5, so the area is 1.
y-m-65-12.s.s3.because.model.1: A probability is the area obtained by gathering the density over an interval, so the density value itself may exceed 1. The shorter the length of the interval, the larger the height can be.
